summary: Defines a set of managed objects, in the Management Information Base used by SNMP, for monitoring and managing MAC bridges that follow the IEEE 802.1D standard and link LAN segments together. It was replaced by RFC 4188.

plainLanguage.summary: A bridge joins two small networks. This memo gives a list of dials and gauges, so a manager can check on a bridge from far away.

questions: how to manage 802.1d bridges with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and managing IEEE 802.1D MAC bridges

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to monitor and manage MAC bridges that connect LAN segments, but the Internet Management Framework lacked objects specifically for bridge management following the IEEE 802.1D standard.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module with objects organized into five groups: a mandatory base group for all bridges, plus optional groups for the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), transparent bridging, static MAC filtering, and source routing. Each group exposes counters, configuration parameters, and status information that SNMP clients can query and in some cases modify.
tldr.outcome: This became the standard way to manage bridges via SNMP for decades. RFC 4188 obsoleted it to update the definitions and improve consistency, but the concepts and structure remain widely understood.

facts.label: Optional groups
facts.value: 4 (STP, transparent bridging, static filtering, source routing)

today: RFC 1493 is a Draft Standard published in July 1993. It was obsoleted by RFC 4188 in September 2005, which updated the MIB definitions for consistency with modern SNMP and bridging standards, added support for additional bridge types, and improved the specification. However, the concepts and structure defined in RFC 1493 remain the foundation for bridge management via SNMP.

sections.title: Bridges Connect Network Segments
sections.content:
A bridge is a network device that connects two or more LAN segments (such as Ethernet segments) at the data-link layer (Layer 2). Unlike routers, which forward packets based on IP addresses and require understanding of network-layer protocols, bridges forward frames based on MAC (Media Access Control) addresses and operate transparently to the network layer.

The IEEE 802.1D standard defines the behavior of MAC bridges, including the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) used to prevent loops in bridged networks. This RFC defines SNMP managed objects for monitoring and managing bridges that implement the IEEE 802.1D standard. Operators can use these objects to observe bridge operation, verify STP convergence, monitor port status, and view the bridge's learned MAC address table.
sections.plainLanguage: A bridge is like a switchboard operator connecting two phone lines. Managers need to be able to check from far away that it is working and to adjust settings.

sections.title: Five Groups: Base, STP, Transparent, Static, and Source Route
sections.content:
The Bridge MIB is organized into five groups, each with a different purpose. The dot1dBase group is mandatory for all bridges and contains information common to any bridge: the bridge's MAC address, the number of ports, the bridge type (transparent, source route, or hybrid SRT), and a generic port table with per-port discards.

The dot1dStp group is optional and contains objects related to the Spanning Tree Protocol. It includes bridge-level parameters like priority and timers (MaxAge, HelloTime, ForwardDelay), the designation of the root bridge, the cost to reach the root, and per-port STP state, priority, and path cost. Operators use this group to monitor STP convergence and adjust STP parameters.

The dot1dTp group covers transparent bridging and includes a Filtering Database (FDB) that maps learned MAC addresses to ports, plus per-port transparent-bridging counters (frames in, frames out, discards).

The dot1dStatic group allows management of static MAC address entries used for filtering: entries can be created to force traffic to specific ports or to block traffic for certain addresses.

The dot1dSr group is reserved for source-route bridging, which is documented separately.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a basic section about the bridge itself, a section about loop prevention (the Spanning Tree), a section about learning where addresses are, a section for manually setting rules, and a section for an older type of bridging.

sections.title: The Spanning Tree Protocol and Loop Prevention
sections.content:
In a bridged network with multiple paths, frames could loop endlessly if the bridge simply forwarded every frame to every port. The Spanning Tree Protocol solves this by having bridges negotiate to disable certain ports (put them into a blocking state) so that only one active path remains between any two LAN segments. STP runs continuously, so if a link fails, the protocol re-converges to reactivate a backup port.

The STP section of the MIB allows operators to observe this process. The dot1dStpDesignatedRoot object shows which bridge is the root of the spanning tree. The dot1dStpRootCost and dot1dStpRootPort indicate the cost and interface of the path to the root as seen from this bridge. Per-port objects indicate each port's STP state (disabled, blocking, listening, learning, or forwarding), priority, and path cost. The RFC defines these costs with reference to IEEE 802.1D: an Ethernet port typically has a default cost of 100, though operators can override this for tuning.

The RFC also includes timer configuration objects (MaxAge, HelloTime, ForwardDelay) and counters for topology changes, allowing operators to verify STP is functioning and to detect network instability.
sections.plainLanguage: The Spanning Tree Protocol finds one path and blocks the others to prevent loops. The MIB lets the manager see which bridge is in charge, what the path looks like, and if the path has changed recently.

sections.title: Transparent Bridging and the Filtering Database
sections.content:
In transparent bridging, the bridge learns the source MAC address of frames as they arrive on each port, building a table that maps MAC addresses to ports. When a frame with a known destination MAC arrives, the bridge forwards it only to the port associated with that address. If the destination is unknown, the frame is flooded to all ports except the arrival port, allowing it to reach its destination.

The dot1dTp group exposes this Filtering Database (FDB) via the dot1dTpFdbTable object. Each entry contains a MAC address, the port it was learned on, and the status (dynamic or static). The dot1dTpAgingTime parameter controls how long a dynamically learned entry is kept before being forgotten; the RFC specifies a range of 10 to 1,000,000 hundredths of a second (10 ms to 10,000 seconds). Operators use this table to verify the bridge has learned addresses correctly and to troubleshoot connectivity issues.

The dot1dTp group also includes per-port counters: the number of frames received, forwarded, and discarded on each port, as well as a counter for entries removed from the FDB due to database overflow.
sections.plainLanguage: The bridge remembers which addresses are on which ports, and the manager can look at that table to understand what the bridge has learned. The manager can also see how busy each port is and set how long the bridge remembers old addresses.

sections.title: Static Filtering and Manual Control
sections.content:
While the bridge dynamically learns MAC addresses, operators sometimes need to manually control how traffic is handled. The dot1dStatic group provides a table where operators can create static entries that override learned behavior. Each entry specifies a MAC address, the port(s) where that address is allowed to send frames (or zero to block the address entirely), and whether the entry is permanent or temporary.

This mechanism allows operators to manually configure MAC-level filtering rules, such as preventing devices from communicating across certain ports or prioritizing traffic for specific devices. These static entries take precedence over dynamically learned entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The manager can write rules saying 'traffic from this MAC address can only use this port' or 'never forward traffic from this MAC address.' These rules override what the bridge learns on its own.
